newsitem.title: GEORGIA: FEATURE - Abkhazia's space monkeys caught in conflict zone.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Abkhazia's space monkeys caught in conflict zone.

text.p: In better days the chimps of Abkhazia's primate research centre were pioneering Soviet cosmonauts, travelling to space and back in missions deemed too risky for man.
Now they gaze out out from rundown cages, casual victims of Abkhazia's bloody ethnic war and its legacy which has reduced their numbers from 2,500 to 300 in four years.
The cliffside institute, the first of its kind in the world when it was founded in 1927, was once a crown jewel in the huge Soviet scientific effort.

It prepared residents like "Proud" and "Devoted" for space missions, two monkeys whose toothy smiles now adorn the walls of a small museum in photographs, along with mines, shell casings and empty rocket shells.
The centre also carried out medical and behavioural studies, testing everything from the first polio vaccines to antibiotics for every conceivable illness.

"Now the only research we can do is how primates react to extreme conditions -- bombing, cold and hunger," said Vakhtang Kakubava, deputy director of the Scientific Research Institute of Experimental Pathology and Therapy, the centre's convoluted official name.
BACKGROUND TO CONFLICT

Abkhazia's palm-fringed Black Sea beaches were once the favourite haunt of the Soviet elite. But when the superpower disintegrated, years of mistrust between ethnic Georgians and Abkhaz erupted into open warfare.

Ragtag Georgian military units marched into the region in 1992 in an attempt to put down demands by the local parliament for more autonomy. The intervention set off a year of fighting in which 10,000 people were killed.

Abkhazia separatist fighters, with Russian military help, then drove Tbilisi's troops out and around 200,000 Georgians, once 45 percent of the population, fled fearing ethnic cleansing and most are now refugees.
The monkeys, whose home has a dramatic view of the sea, ended up on the front lines between Georgians and Abkhaz, as the bullet-ridden, shell-damaged buildings of the complex show.
Georgian soldiers made off with several hundred monkeys as "trophies". Others, including some rare species, were sold abroad for thousands of dollars each.
"Some forced our workers to bring them the monkeys, then they would ride off with them in tanks. They lived in the barracks as mascots," said Kakubava.
MONKEYS KILLED IN FIGHTING

When the Abkhaz shelled Sukhumi with artillery and multiple rocket launchers in an attempt to retake the city, some of the animals died from shrapnel and gunshot wounds. Others were killed when the institute took direct artillery hits.
A special group of about 100 monkeys which had been released into a special conservation area also ended up near the front lines, and some of them were killed by anti-personnel mines.

The rest fled the fighting like human refugees and headed north towards Abkhazia's snow-capped mountains. They have not returned since hostiltites died down in 1993 despite the far colder environment in their forced exile.

"It isn't their usual habitat but they've adjusted quite well. Sometimes you can see groups of them sunning themselves on cliffs. They live in abandoned villages destroyed in the war and eat fruit off the trees or catch rats," said Kakubava.
But the winter following the Abkhaz takeover was just as bad for the monkeys as the ordeal of the war and scores died of cold, disease, and hunger.
Workers collected tangerines from abandoned orchards to try to prevent starvation, but it was often not enough.
Other monkeys bear psychological scars. Some, like 15-year-old Charlie are more afraid of men than women.

"A lot of the soldiers came in here and fired their weapons into the air for a laugh to frighten the animals. They still react to any loud noise as if it's a shot or a bomb," said Ira, a worker at the center, as Charlie slunk shyly away.

The international community has not recognised Abkhaz independence and Georgia and Russia have imposed a partial blockade to try to bring it to heel. Travel to the region is difficult and the curbs affect the scientists too.
"This has cut us off from the world scientific community. They think we don't exist anymore, and we have few sources of financing" said Kakubava.
Kakubava said shipments of food aid destined for the monkeys from a German organisation were often held up by Russian border guards who demanded large bribes.
In recent months the population decline has been somewhat stemmed but the situation is far from normal. "We are just keeping them alive," he said.

Kakubava, one of a small minority of ethnic Georgians who stayed in the local capital Sukhumi after the Abkhaz moved in, has an Abkhaz wife and felt at first hand the supercharged environment of ethnic war and its effect on mixed families.
"In that, I like the monkeys better than humans, they have no nationalities question," he said.
